Concept 05

Distributed Runner

The same Pipeline, run by several processes at once against different slices of the same data. Coordination is a lease on a row range; durability is Arrow IPC bytes in an embedded database.

In one line
Many nodes, one pipeline, at-least-once per row range
You need
pcs-service with distributed; add distributed-raft for a cluster
Read this if
One process is not enough, and you need work to survive a node dying halfway through a batch

The claim loop

DistributedRunner holds three things: a store, a Box<dyn PipelineRuntime> used as a template, and a RunnerConfig. Calling run(world_factory) starts a loop that claims work, runs the template against it, persists the result, and acknowledges. Then it goes back for more, until the store says there is nothing pending.

The claim is the whole mechanism. PartitionSource::claim_next_batch hands back a BatchClaim: a batch_id, a half-open Range<u32> of rows, a fresh claim_id, and a lease that expires at a wall-clock millisecond. Hold the lease and the range is yours. Lose it and somebody else gets the same rows.

claims, leases, coordination rows and Arrow IPC bytes

Two lease mechanisms keep the window narrow. Before the run, should_renew checks whether less than 30 % of the TTL (or ten seconds, whichever is smaller) remains, and renews if so. During the run a renewal task sits beside run_on_with_state in the same tokio::select!, renewing at TTL/3. If a renewal fails the select resolves on the renewal branch, the run is cancelled at its next await point, and the claim is released rather than acked. A runner never keeps working on a lease it has lost.

The same is true after the run. If the checkpoint write fails, or the accumulator save fails, or the state blob save fails, the runner calls release_claim and skips the ack. Nothing is acknowledged that could not be made durable.

The runner does not load your rows

world_factory is called once per claim and whatever it returns is what the pipeline sees. The runner never reads the master batch's Arrow IPC back out of the store. Registering the components and filling in the rows for claim.row_range is your closure's job. See examples/distributed_fulfillment/store.rs, which wraps the store to intercept claim_next_batch and stash the IPC where the factory can reach it.

Standalone and clustered

Both modes use the same two traits and the same runner. Only the store construction differs.

FeatureWhat it adds
distributed PartitionSource, CheckpointStore, DistributedRunner, and RedbSharedStore::single_node — one redb file, commands applied directly, no quorum.
distributed-raft openraft on top: ArrowRedbLogStore, ArrowRedbStateMachine, the snapshot codec, the TCP transport, ArrowRaftDriver, and RedbSharedStore::multi_node.
service-cluster service plus distributed-raft — what the pcs-service binary needs to run mode "cluster" from a config file.

RedbSharedStore is an enum, not a trait object. The SingleNode variant owns an Arc<Database>; the MultiNode variant deliberately owns no database at all, only the state machine's shared handle for reads and a Raft driver handle for writes. The type system is what stops a clustered node from quietly applying a command to its local file.

Publishing work

A master batch is a registered chunk of Arrow IPC with an id, a component name, a schema version, and a row count. Runners never create batches; they consume them.

Rustfive arguments, in this order
store
    .register_master_batch(
        0,                         // batch_id: u64
        Order::name().to_string(), // component: String
        1,                         // schema_id: u32
        ipc_bytes,                 // Vec<u8>, an Arrow IPC stream
        900,                       // total_rows: u32
    )
    .await?;

Claim granularity follows directly from how a pending range is found. The state machine collects every Claimed or Completed range for the batch and returns the first row not covered by one. For a freshly registered batch that is 0..total_rows, the whole thing. So a second node does not get half of batch 0; it gets batch 1. Parallelism is a function of how many batches you register, and how big you make them.

That is also why the 1 MiB cap matters at ingestion time. MAX_LOG_ENTRY_BYTES is 1024 * 1024, and register_master_batch rejects anything larger before it can reach Raft. Split the input into several batch_ids and you get durable log entries and cross-node parallelism from the same decision.

Running one node

Single-node mode is a real deployment, not a toy: one process, one redb file, every command applied straight to it. It is also the shortest path to seeing the loop work.

Rustfeature = "distributed"
use std::path::Path;

use pcs_service::PcsResult;
use pcs_service::component::Component;
use pcs_service::dataset::Dataset;
use pcs_service::distributed::RedbSharedStore;
use pcs_service::distributed::runner::{DistributedRunner, RunnerConfig};
use pcs_service::distributed::strategy::CheckpointStrategy;
use pcs_service::pipeline::Pipeline;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> PcsResult<()> {
    // One redb file. No Raft, no second database, no quorum.
    let store = RedbSharedStore::single_node(Path::new("/var/lib/pcs/pcs.redb"))?;

    let (ipc_bytes, total_rows) = encode_orders_ipc()?;
    store
        .register_master_batch(0, Order::name().to_string(), 1, ipc_bytes, total_rows)
        .await?;

    // A template. Its own dataset, sources and sinks are never used — each
    // claim runs against whatever `world_factory` hands back.
    let template = Pipeline::builder("order-processor")
        .with::<Order>()
        .with_system(ValidateOrder)
        .with_system(PriceOrder)
        .build();

    let runner = DistributedRunner::new(
        store,
        Box::new(template),
        RunnerConfig {
            checkpoint_strategy: CheckpointStrategy::EveryStage,
            schema_id: 1,
            max_batches: None,
            ..Default::default()
        },
    );

    // Called once per claim. Register the components and load the rows here.
    let processed = runner.run(hydrate_partition).await?;
    println!("{processed} batches acked");
    Ok(())
}

run returns the number of batches it acked. It stops when claim_next_batch returns None, or when max_batches is reached. For a long-lived service use run_with_shutdown, which takes a CancellationToken and exits between batches without holding a lease.

Where state lives

A clustered node keeps two redb files side by side. Only one of them is agreed on by the cluster; the other is a local consequence of applying it.

replicated coordination state Arrow IPC payloads produced inside the processor

All three checkpoint kinds share one table and one API. They are told apart by stage_idx, and the two reserved values sit far above any real stage index, which numbers from zero and stays in the dozens.

ConstantValuePayload
— 0 The whole partition Dataset, written by the runner after the run.
PROCESSOR_STATE_STAGE_SENTINEL u32::MAX - 1 Whatever run_on_with_state returned. Opaque to the host.
ACCUMULATOR_STAGE_SENTINEL u32::MAX The WindowAccumulator component alone, via write_component_ipc.
The stage checkpoint is write-only, and there is one of it

The runner calls run_on_with_state once per claim, since the runtime runs its own stages internally, then writes a single checkpoint at stage_idx = 0. Nothing reads it back: recovery re-runs the batch from the top rather than resuming mid-pipeline. Two consequences. CheckpointStrategy::EveryNStages(n) only ever fires for n == 1, because the sole call is should_checkpoint(0). And the checkpoint is an artefact for an operator or an external reader, not a resume point.

Wiring a cluster

ArrowRaftDriver::start is async, takes the two database paths, and returns the handle plus the driver's task. Keep the task alive for the life of the process.

Rustfeature = "distributed-raft"
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::Arc;

use pcs_service::distributed::RedbSharedStore;
use pcs_service::distributed::consensus::{ArrowRaftDriver, ArrowRaftDriverConfig};

// Opens both redb files and refuses to start if the state machine is behind
// what the log store has already purged.
let (handle, _driver_task) = ArrowRaftDriver::start(
    ArrowRaftDriverConfig {
        node_id: 1,
        listen_addr: "0.0.0.0:9001".parse().unwrap(),
        // "host:port" strings, resolved lazily at connect time, so Docker
        // service names work. An empty map auto-initialises a single node.
        peers: HashMap::from([
            (2, "pcs-2:9001".to_string()),
            (3, "pcs-3:9001".to_string()),
        ]),
        heartbeat_interval_ms: 50,
        election_timeout_min_ms: 150,
        election_timeout_max_ms: 300,
    },
    data_dir.join("raft-log.redb"),      // openraft log store
    data_dir.join("cluster-app.redb"),   // applied state
)
.await?;

// `start` wires outbound connections only. Without this listener peers cannot
// deliver votes or heartbeats and no leader is ever elected.
let _tcp_server = handle.spawn_tcp_server("0.0.0.0:9001".parse().unwrap());

// Reads lock the very database the state machine writes to — no second file
// handle. Mutations are proposed through Raft.
let store = RedbSharedStore::multi_node(Arc::clone(handle.app_db()), handle.clone());

From here the runner code is byte-for-byte the single-node code: same template, same RunnerConfig, same runner.run(...). Only the store changed.

One node bootstraps the cluster once, with handle.initialize(members) over a BTreeMap<u64, openraft::BasicNode>; a second call is swallowed as a no-op. Because BasicNode comes from openraft and PCS pins =0.10.0-alpha.17, a crate calling initialize directly has to match that pin. The pcs-service binary does all of this from a config file under mode "cluster", so hand-rolling it is only for embedding the runner in your own process.

You do not have to route work to the leader. A proposal made on a follower comes back as ForwardToLeader, and the driver forwards it over the same TCP transport using the address from its peers map. Every propose is wrapped in a 30-second timeout, so an unreachable leader surfaces as a retryable cluster propose timeout (30s) rather than a hang.

What refuses to start

Immediately after opening the log store and the state machine, ArrowRaftDriver::start reads log_state.last_purged_log_id and the state machine's last_applied, and hands both to validate_store_consistency. It returns an error, and the node does not start, in two cases:

  • The log store has purged up to some index but the state machine reports last_applied = None.
  • The state machine's last_applied.index is behind the log store's purge watermark.

Both mean the log and the application file did not come from the same node at the same moment. The usual cause is restoring the two files from different backups, or wiping raft-log.redb while keeping cluster-app.redb. Failing at startup avoids a replica that diverges quietly.

State that outlives a batch

A native Pipeline keeps everything it knows in the Dataset, so the default run_on_with_state ignores prior, delegates to run_on, and returns Ok(None). Nothing extra is persisted.

A WASM processor cannot do that. Every call gets a fresh wasmtime Store, so processor linear memory does not survive a batch. That is deliberate: a trapped instance cannot corrupt anything that outlives it. The one channel left is the return value:

Rustthe host seam, from pcs-core
async fn run_on_with_state(
    &self,
    data: &mut Dataset,
    prior: Option<&[u8]>,
) -> PcsResult<Option<Vec<u8>>>;

WasmPipelineRuntime passes prior straight into the processor's run-batch export and returns the checkpoint field of the result. The runner stores that blob under PROCESSOR_STATE_STAGE_SENTINEL and hands it back as the next call's prior. On the processor side, one macro form opts in:

Rustin the processor crate
// Stateless: `prior` is ignored, `checkpoint` is always None.
pcs_processor::export_pipeline!(build);

// Stateful: systems read and write a `ProcessorState<Counter>` resource, and
// whatever they leave in it becomes the next batch's `prior`.
pcs_processor::export_pipeline!(build, state = Counter);

The pointer to the newest blob is a chain, not a fixed key: the blob is written under the claim that produced it and read back under the id of the claim that wrote the previous one, because the state machine resolves a checkpoint's batch_id through the claims table and rejects a write whose uuid is not a live claim. Reads survive the ack, so the chain holds for as long as the runner loop does. A runner that restarts hands the runtime None, so the processor starts cold and rebuilds its state.
